This page documents my use of generative AI for the
[Class 5 note](class5.qmd), following the course AI policy.

## Tool and scope

Two tools were used, on different parts of the work.

| Tool | Date | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| **OpenAI Codex** desktop assistant, GPT-6 family (the exact build was not shown in the session) | October 7, 2026 | The first English draft, source checks, the base R overfitting simulation, and the Quarto page |
| **Claude** (Anthropic), model `claude-opus-5`, Claude desktop app | October 6–7, 2026 | A Traditional Chinese reading guide to the two Google Flu papers, before I read them; then editing my revision of sections (a)–(c) down to the word limit |

## User prompt

The user supplied the Chinese reading guide `GFT_Ginsberg2009_Lazer2014_中文導讀.md` and this request:

> Post one note as a Quarto page on your GitHub website (about one page, 500–700 words), in your own words and with sources cited, in three short sections:
> a. Big data analytics pitfalls. Use Google Flu Trends as your case. Address at least “big data hubris,” algorithm dynamics (the data-generating process changes under you), and transparency and replicability.
> b. Overfitting and overparameterization. Define both and explain how they apply to Google Flu Trends (millions of candidate search terms screened against a limited set of CDC flu observations). Optional bonus: include one R chart that shows overfitting, e.g., training vs. test error as polynomial degree increases.
> c. Wickham talk summary (from item 2b).
> 幫我做這些

## Sources and verification limits

The course preparation PDF identified the assigned EMBL keynote. The assistant consulted the original Ginsberg publication page and the full Lazer paper, checked the video description and chapter navigation, and inspected selected on-screen demonstrations. YouTube did not provide an exportable transcript; the assistant did not review the complete spoken lecture. The talk summary in the first draft was therefore limited to the observed workflow and demonstrations. I have since watched the lecture myself and rewritten that section; see below.

The draft distinguishes candidate feature screening from the final regression's coefficient count, avoids claiming that overparameterization guarantees overfitting, and treats search-platform changes as plausible contributors rather than a proven single cause. The chart is an original fixed-seed simulation, not empirical Google or CDC data. No earlier student's work is used as a source.

## Revision after reading and watching

The page began as an AI-generated draft, and I did not want to submit it in that
state. I then read Ginsberg et al. (2009) and Lazer et al. (2014) in full and
watched the keynote, and revised all three sections from my own notes:

- **(a)** I added the two concrete transparency facts — the 45 search terms were
  never published, and Google Correlate does not return the example terms given
  in the GFT papers.
- **(b)** I added my own case: concatenating features from several deep learning
  backbones for a medical-imaging classifier, where training performance was
  excellent and test performance got worse. The example is mine; the parallel to
  the GFT ratio is the point I wanted to make with it.
- **(c)** I rewrote the section entirely. The earlier version listed the
  technologies named in the talk; this one reports the two demonstrations I
  actually watched (the gganimate render and the R Markdown knit), the
  exploratory/expositional distinction, and the remark at 20:08 that the only
  way to make good visualizations is to make many bad ones. The pushback is also
  new and is my own: tidy data as a compulsory first stage assumes a table of
  observations and variables, which is not the shape of the tensor and matrix
  data I work with.

Claude edited the revised wording and cut it to the word limit. The arguments,
the example, and the objection in section (c) are mine.
